rv.q: For me, seeing “Fat Ham,” even multiple times, thus remains a revelation and a balm.
Not to mention that "Fat Ham" is a total gas — the funniest and most invigorating new show on Broadway
James Ijames has created a brilliant contemporary riff on 'Hamlet' that crackles with wit, wisdom and emotional truth.
At no point does this play feel like anything other than a big-fun Broadway show: it’s a smart, fearless and often wildly entertaining 90 minutes, filled with radical ideas and absurdist spectacle.
Fat Ham is an exhilarating example of Ijames's world-building, his prowess for merriment and lyrical musing.
Fat Ham is a riot of a play that manages to be both hilarious and deeply moving.

James Ijames' Pulitzer Prize-winning play 'Fat Ham' is a raucous, irreverent and ultimately moving riff on 'Hamlet' that brings Shakespeare's tragedy into a contemporary Black family's backyard barbecue.

Its rhythm can be hard to detect, but once you find it — in Pap’s barbed commands, in Larry’s circumspect admissions, in Tedra’s agitated denials and in Juicy’s near-hopeful judgements — you’ll be glad you came to the cookout.

James Ijames's Pulitzer Prize-winning play, a riff on 'Hamlet' set at a family barbecue in North Carolina, is both funny and deeply felt, though it occasionally strains under the weight of its own ambitions.
Fat Ham serves an endless tray of delight but every bit of sparkle added ironically dulls the play's brilliance.
Conceptually, I'm right there with what Ijames is cooking up, but by the time that finale came around, I was left a little cold.
Much of Ijames’ “Fat Ham” is playful ideas that don’t add up.
‘Fat Ham,’ James Ijames’ clever contemporary queer take on Hamlet, is not a tragedy.
“Fat Ham” is the most fun you’ll have at any play this Broadway season.
Change is possible; we just must want to do it.
By turns sweet and saucy (and very funny), the play stays just close enough to Hamlet to keep us off-balance.
It’s certainly not the kind of catharsis you’d expect from an Elizabethan tragedy, but like the production itself, it’s scrumptious and utterly satisfying.

But Ijames’s surprising finale, a feisty twist of theatrical rule-breaking, soars on the Broadway stage, reclaiming the narrative away from Shakespeare, away from the cultural constrictions of the American South, and celebrates the play’s characters in all their hammy, juicy humanity.
Ijames' characters are as American as pulled pork and baby back ribs, which emphasizes the universality of Shakespeare's work.

He also delivers what is perhaps the single most memorable moment in “Fat Ham,” a long soliloquy (very much not Shakespearean) about a dream encounter that climaxes in, um, sexual congress with a gingerbread man cookie.

While the play (which runs just under two hours without intermission) does drag at times, it makes for a fresh, fast and loose adaptation with a keen awareness of masculinity, violence, and family dysfunction.
For his part, Marcel Spears as Juicy might bring to mind another Black, hefty, gay, and moody character, namely Usher from Michael R. Jackson's A Strange Loop.
Funny and thought-provoking as it is, Fat Ham feels like the second-to-last draft of something better.
It takes that play, messes with it, f**ks it up the ass, and soars.
You don't have to be an expert Hamlet to thoroughly enjoy Fat Ham, but the more you do know, the richer the experience is bound to be.
Just be careful you don’t die laughing while watching it.
Simply put, for Ijames’ insightfully idiosyncratic take on Hamlet, we’re not in Elsinore anymore, and that’s a good thing.

“Fat Ham” may not be all that one might expect from a Pulitzer-winning work, but the audience enjoyed this zippy production which offers lighthearted laughs, colorful characters and a brisk tempo—all thanks to Ali’s beyond the proscenium staging.
Fat Ham simply doesn't cut as deeply as, say, A Strange Loop, the previous winner, which tackles similar themes.
